blocks.p: Rei started with the sixth name because Higuchi had starred it twice in the climbing margin. Watanabe Jun, Despair VI, weakening. A weakening seat was the one place where the registry stopped being a page and became a person. A person Rei could ruin or save by knocking on the wrong door.

The pencilled note sent him to Itabashi, to the quiet part of it near Tokiwadai. It was a district of planned streets laid out in the 1930s, straight and tidy, where very little happened on the other side. Gin's book called that kind of ground clean. The Grid kept safe houses there for practitioners who needed to read without noise. Rei understood at once why a man carrying Despair would choose to live in the quietest ground he could find.

Watanabe Jun was not what Rei had braced for. Rei had been carrying the word holder around like a weight. Watanabe Jun was a slight man in a cardigan two sizes too big, shelving returns at a municipal library. He looked fifty. His file said thirty-five. He had the particular gentleness of a person who has decided not to take up much room in the world.

Rei stood in the periodicals with a borrowed newspaper and watched him for an hour. The only strange thing about him was that the light near him was wrong. It was dimmer by a half-step, the way a room dims when an unseen cloud passes a window no one can find. And no one ever quite met his eyes. Not the student asleep over his books. Not the woman returning her romance novels.
Watching him reshelve a novel with both hands, as if it were heavier than it was, Rei understood that he was looking at the cost written plain.

A held domain was not a power Watanabe used. It was a weather he stood in so that no one else had to. Despair was the one he had drawn, by whatever lottery or inheritance or terrible volunteering the registry ran on. It had thinned him the way water thins a stone. Not dramatically. Just continuously. Until the man was mostly the shape of the thing he carried, with a little person left over to do the carrying.

Higuchi's word was weakening, and now Rei could see it. There was a tremor in how he held the books. There was a translucence at the edges of him in the bad library light. He looked like a seam being pressed from the wrong side by an empty chair two wards over. He was not failing because he was old. He was failing because the thirteenth seat was pulling, and his was the office nearest the wound, and for six years the vacant chair had been borrowing his strength to lean with.

He caught Rei watching, finally, the way the haunted always do. Rei expected fear. Instead Watanabe gave him a small tired nod. It was recognition, not of Rei's face, but of his kind. The kind that could see the dimmed light.
He came over and spoke very quietly, so that the sleeping student would not wake.

"I've been wondering when one of you would come," he said. "If you have a moment, and you are what I think you are, I'd like to know something. On the worst nights I've started to feel a thirteenth weight leaning on my sixth. And I've started to feel that something kind and patient, over in Kita, has begun very gently to help it lean. Is that true?"

Rei had not come to tell a dying man the name of the thing killing him. But this man was holding Despair for the whole north of the city, and he had asked a true question. The cardigan was two sizes too big because there was less of him inside it every week.
"Yes," Rei said. "It's true. The thing helping it lean is wearing my brother."
Watanabe closed his eyes for a moment. When he opened them there was no surprise in them. Only a kind of tired thanks.
"Then I'm sorry for you," he said. "That's worse than what's happening to me."

Rei could not visit all twelve. There was not time. Some of the names lived in places he had no road into. One of them, the eleventh, Park Junho, Longing, was listed at the community centre in Shin-Ōkubo, with a note in Gin's hand that Rei did not yet understand. Pak Sun-ja keeps his secret. What secret, the note did not say.
But he saw four more before the trains started again. Once he knew how to look for a leaning chair, he could not stop seeing them, and the city rearranged itself around the seeing.

In Kita, down an alley behind a public bath, a boiler-room door stood propped open for the heat. Inside, a big grey-haired man in dark clothes was feeding a firebox one shovel at a time. Every movement was banked down to the minimum. No wasted gesture. No slammed door. Rei did not go in. He was not even sure he had found the right man, because Gin's file said the second seat was hard to find on purpose. But he watched the man work for a long minute, and it looked like a whole life built into one shape, a shape that gave the weather he carried somewhere to go that hurt no one. The heat poured off the firebox and never once reached his hands. It looked like a holder who had made his peace. Even so, while Rei watched, he glanced north twice, the way a man checks a sky he does not trust.

blocks.cap: Hoshino Haru, holder of Joy, at his stockpot

blocks.p: On Sakae Street the light was on in a small noodle shop at two in the morning. Through the steamed glass Rei could see a stocky man in an apron skimming a stockpot. The broth took eight hours, Gin had written. Hoshino Haru, Joy, the seventh seat. The cleanest succession on record. Rei stood across the street and simply felt it for a while. It was the warmest thing he had felt all month, the plain satisfaction of something good done well. And even here, the steam from the pot drifted north when there was no wind to carry it.

Outside a pale danchi he looked up and saw a woman sitting on the half-landing of an outside stairwell at three in the morning, her knees drawn up, not climbing. Fear, the fourth seat, had not climbed her own stairs in days.
Near Ueno station a lean man paid for a plate he had not finished and was gone before his change was counted. Hunger, the ninth, never stayed anywhere long enough to finish a plate.
Each of them was ordinary in the same specific way. Each was a person who had organised a whole self around a thing that could not be put down.
And each of them, Rei came to understand over that long night, was leaning the same way.
Not toward each other. Toward the gap.

A held registry should balance. Twelve disciplines spread round a table, so that no single seam took more than it could bear. For a century, Higuchi's note said, it had balanced. But a table with one chair pulled out is a table that tilts, and every plate on it slides, slowly, toward the empty place.

The man at the boiler checked the northern sky because Rage felt the pull of the vacancy as a heat that would not bank all the way down. The woman on the stairs felt it as a fear with no object. Watanabe felt it most, because his seat was the nearest and the weakest. But all of them felt it, all twelve. A low constant draw toward Kita, where a chair had stood open since the year the city went grey. Not one of them had the standing to fill it. Not one of them was free to leave their own. And not one of them, Rei realised, had ever been told why their lifelong weather had lately been getting worse.

The first bakery on the night-bus route opened at five. Rei had not eaten. He stood outside the Akebono Bakery by the station while a woman in her late fifties raised the shutter and set out the first trays. The window glowed.

A man was already waiting. He was neat, unremarkable, with gold wire glasses and a collar one button open. The baker handed him a paper bag without being asked, and he thanked her, and for the few seconds she spoke to him she looked like the only person in the world. Then Rei saw that it went the other way too. The man was looking at her as if she were the only person in the world. It was not performed. It was simply what his attention did.
Sakuma Kei, Rei thought. Love. The third seat. The most stable domain of the thirteen. The dawn regular Mrs. Kawai fed.

Kei walked past him on the pavement. For a moment he glanced at Rei through the gold frames, with an odd, kind attention, as if he had just recognised the shape of some bond Rei carried. Then he nodded politely and went on toward the station. He did not look north at all. Rei would remember that. The steadiest of them did not look north. He just walked a little faster.
Rei stood on the last bridge before full light with the registry copied into the back of Gin's book. Twelve names, twelve weathers, and one wound.
What frightened him was not how strong the far shore was. It was how reasonable the Healer's plan looked from here.

Twelve people were being slowly crushed by an empty chair. As far as Rei could read it that night, one demon, patient and kind, was proposing to end the leaning. To fill the gap. To let Watanabe put down a weight that was killing him. To let the man at the boiler bank his furnace all the way at last.

And the price? The thing in the chair would not be a person carrying an emotion inward for the city's sake. It would be an emotion wearing a person outward for its own. The body it meant to do this in was Gin's. The hand it had spent a month keying to fit the seat was Rei's.

The trap had never been that the plan was evil. The trap was that, seen from a bridge at dawn with a dying librarian behind him, the plan looked like mercy. Rei was the only one placed to refuse it. And refusing it would leave twelve people leaning into a gap he had just told one of them was real.
